newsitem.title: UK: SFO accused of contempt of court in Sumitomo case.
newsitem.headline: SFO accused of contempt of court in Sumitomo case.

text.p: Five top members of the Serious Fraud Office (SFO), including outgoing director George Staple, were accused of contempt of court on Monday at a hearing in London's High Court.

They were accused of breaching a court order banning them from obtaining information from computers seized and not returned under search warrants issued regarding the Sumitomo Corp copper fraud investigation.

The six computers were seized in a raid on the Loom Lane, Radlett, Hertfordshire premises of Kay Accountants Ltd on December 6, 1996 after the issue by City of London Magistrates Court the day before of "search and seize" warrants.
Later the same day Kay director, Jeffrey Green obtained a temporary High Court order - made permanent on December 10 - banning the SFO from downloading the seized computers and ordering their return.
But on Monday, QC Alan Jones told two of the country's senior judges Lord Justice Staughton and Justice Scott Baker that the SFO continued to download information, despite the order.
"They got the terms of the order at eight minutes past six," Jones said, referring to the events of December 6.
However, despite the court ban the SFO continued "imaging" the computers until later that evening after the terms of the ban were made known to them, he said.
Now, committal moves are being taken against Staple, SFO lawyers Andrew Jackson and Christopher Walker, accountant Anne Dilks and computer expert Michael Hainey.

After the committal proceedings have been completed the court will then be asked to deal with an application for a judicial review of the "search and seize" order granted by the magistrates and exemplary damages will also be sought.
It is to be argued that the order was far too wide. Jones told the court there was a strong argument that the warrant granted to the SFO was too widely drawn and was therefore invalid.
He said there had been a failure to explain the full situation to the magistrates, with the result that the SFO had intended to download everything fron the seized computers.
"We say removal of everything in the computers is on any view completely outside the terms of the warrant," Jones added.
Britain's SFO is investigating a multi-billion dollar scandal that rocked world metal markets last year. It is liaising with investigators in Japan.
In June last year, Japanese conglomerate Sumitomo fired its head copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he was a rogue who admitted running up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading.
